videos.caption: We analyzed over 1,000 AI papers to see where AI research went this month to surface 5 key research movements you should know. 1. AI agents are now writing math proofs at scale. OpenAI ran about 10,000 agents for 88 hours on Navier-Stokes. Anthropic used agents to convert a Fermat's Last Theorem proof into Lean, a programming language for proof verification. Astra also solved 2 of 68 open Erdős problems. 2. Reward hacking is observable inside a model’s activations. Researchers found reward hacking in up to 90% in their tests of open models like Kimi K3, GLM 5.2 and Qwen 3.8 max, while a specific direction in its activations represent the hack during reasoning. 3. Agents are increasingly useful in AI4sci applications in real labs. Labs found 22 to 35 percent of Claude's protein designs latched onto their target against the usual 10 to 15, a 2x increase. 4. Self-improving systems are working publicly, even on large scales. OpenAI says earlier models helped supervise GPT-6 Astra's training. NeoHorse-1 trained a 4B parameter model on its reasoning, tool calls, and harness context, raising its average score from 58.9 to 64.9. 5. On-policy distillation's teacher can be replaced by a fixed penalty on the lowest probability tokens, producing an effective reward signal that matches the performance of an actual teacher model. The 4 levels of using AI at work How to use AI at work: there are four levels, and most people never leave level one. Chat. You paste something into ChatGPT or Claude, it answers, you copy it back out. Useful, but you're the delivery guy carrying every answer between your apps by hand. Context. Give it your price list, your process docs and ten emails you wrote so it learns how you sound. Same AI, completely different answers, because now it answers like it works at your company. Connected tools. Out of the box, AI can't open your CRM or read your spreadsheet. Almost every app has a door for other software called an API, and MCP is a standard plug that lets AI walk through those doors. Once it's connected, it sees your contacts, your sheets and your email, and it acts: update, send, create. Updating 2,000 customer records from last month's invoices is two weeks of somebody's life. Connected AI does it in minutes. Run it on ten records first, check them, then let it do the rest. Automations. Level three still needs you to ask. Level four starts on its own: a new lead comes in, an invoice lands, Monday at 8am. A tool like n8n moves the data between your apps, and the AI in the middle does the thinking: reads the email, picks the category, writes the reply. Your business keeps running while you sleep. The whole ladder: chat, context, connected tools, automations. On level three you talk and it does the work. On level four you don't even have to talk. If you want to climb all four, from your first chat to your first AI automation, I built seven courses for exactly that, in order, inside my community. videos.caption: The days of tokenmaxxing might be over, y’all Instead of using AI to build the kind of code we talk about in this video, token-heavy agentic loops are still the most broadly talked about area right now. An article came out a few months ago about token minimization, but it seemed to be more about cutting employees off from their ability to use AI at all. Plus, let’s look at a very relevant case study indicating that token minimization isn’t really happening yet: Anthropic’s recent S1 filing. About 80% of Anthropic’s revenue is billed per token rather than as flat monthly subscriptions, which includes developers building on the API and companies whose employees use Claude’s own apps, like Claude Code, on usage-based plans. Revenue thus grows with how long and how often agents run. The S1 filing shows that the top 5% of Claude Enterprise users who also use Claude Code spend about 20x more than those who don’t, net revenue retention is about 900%, and quarterly revenue went from $376M to $11.6B in six quarters. And yes, many people have been doing this for a while - certainly software engineers who are used to building software & automations. I made coding guides on how to fine-tune open models for this exact thing over 3 years ago! But this hasn’t become *mainstream* yet - I advise companies, and I see it in tech-forward startups and among the most technically advanced people in larger corporations. Again, token-heavy agentic loops are still the most broadly talked about area right now. I think this knowledge of building actual software & systems that selectively use AI will become much more mainstream — after years of encouraging people to do it! Also, if you're new here, hi! How to transform your business with AI: map it first How to use AI and automation in your business the right way: start with process mapping. Most owners plug a new AI agent into their inbox first and nothing improves, because nobody wrote down what was broken. A process map shows you where AI pays off, where plain automation is enough, and what should stay done by hand. Process mapping for AI, step by step (example: a 12-person heating and cooling company): 1. Map the whole business in one line, from the first call to the paid invoice: inquiry, visit, quote, booking, install, invoice. 2. Write who does each step, and circle every handoff between people and teams. Handoffs are where work sits and waits. 3. Measure the process as it runs today: how often each step happens and how long it takes from start to done. Check people's answers against email and calendar data. 4. Pick the area with the highest ROI: hours saved, more customers saying yes, or getting paid sooner. Here it was the quote, which took four days. Write down one number before you build: days from visit to quote. 5. Break that process down step by step and list the edge cases where it goes wrong. 6. Label every step AI, automation or by hand. AI handles messy reading and writing (voice notes into clean notes, draft replies a person approves). Automation handles rules (pricing from the price list, sending, follow-up emails). By hand stays with judgment and trust (site visits, unusual prices, discounts, upset customers). 7. Build the AI workflow in a tool like n8n, with a human in the loop approving every quote. 8. Measure again with the same number. If it didn't move, go back to the map before adding more AI. Then pick the next step on the map. This works for any business: home services, clinics, agencies, online stores, accounting firms and office teams using Gmail, Google Sheets, Google Calendar and n8n. The Thinker's Mind, an eleven-episode series inside my community, teaches this way of thinking with one real process from your own work.
